DORIAN.title: Knurling catalogue (technical section)
DORIAN.note: Maker. Teeth = pi D / P (P = 1/TPI); diametral pitch: teeth = D x DP; 30 deg diagonal: teeth = D x DP x cos 30; blank by trial, change by +/- 0.005 in if the knurl double tracks.

HOMMEL_KELLER.title: Zeus knurling catalogue 2021, technical pages 35-46
HOMMEL_KELLER.note: Maker. CP pitch = 25.4 / TPI mm; DP pitch = pi x 25.4 / DP mm; DIN 403 pitches; form knurling enlarges the diameter (empirical table by material and pitch); cut knurling barely changes it.

SHERLINE.title: Knurling tool holder instructions (P/N 3004), 20 TPI knurls
SHERLINE.note: Maker of small lathes. The starting diameter is best found by trial and error on a scrap piece of similar material; change the diameter up or down by about .005 in (printed with '.1 mm' beside it; 0.005 in is 0.127 mm) when the knurl does not come out right; plenty of cutting oil; slow speed, about 100 rpm for 1/2 in diameter of soft material. Its chart of the increase in knurled diameter did not read cleanly and is not used.

GENSWISS.title: Knurling tips
GENSWISS.note: Tool supplier. Tracking is usually settled after one full turn of the part; double tracking can usually be cured by more infeed on bump or cut knurling; bump infeed .001 to .004 in per revolution (0.025 to 0.1 mm), finished in 5 to 20 revolutions; .0005 in of blank variation shows as about .001 in on the knurled diameter; some trial and error is needed; not above about 150 sfm (50 m/min), about 50 sfm (15 m/min) for harder steels and stainless.

HOFFMAN.title: Knurling (notes on getting a knurl to track)
HOFFMAN.note: Personal site of a machinist. Print the knurl, count the lines and measure their span: 75 lines in 3.535 in is 0.0471 in; the blank must be a whole multiple of pitch / pi (0.015 in); 5/8 in stock holds 41, blank 0.615 in. Turn the spindle by hand with mild pressure to get a clean impression, then raise the pressure to full depth; plenty of oil.

PJS_ANSI.title: Knurling: ANSI standard knurls
PJS_ANSI.note: Personal site quoting ANSI/ASME B94.6-1984 (the standard itself was not read). Diametral pitches 64, 96, 128 and 160, 96 preferred; teeth on the work = DP x work diameter (1/2 in at 96 DP is 48); a 3/4 in nominal 96 DP wheel has 72 teeth, major diameter .7440 in, circular pitch .0325 at the outside and .0327 nominal.

PJS_TECH.title: Knurling: techniques
PJS_TECH.note: Same author as the ANSI page, so not an independent second source for it. Get within .001 to .002 in of the calculated diameter; turn the chuck by hand about two full revolutions and inspect for double tracking; lowest speed (150 to 200 rpm); light machine oil on the wheels and pins.

not_used.title: Knowledge base page on knurling cast iron
not_used.why: The page contradicts itself on the sign of the diameter allowance and on its units. Nothing is taken from it.

not_used.title: Chart 'Approximate increase in knurled diameters' in the 3004 instructions
not_used.why: The columns did not come through in order when the PDF was read, so the figures are not tabulated.

trial_steps.t: Take a scrap piece of the same material as the job and chamfer its end.
trial_steps.why: The right blank is best found on scrap of similar material. The chamfer is BenchMate's advice, so the knurl starts on a clean edge.

trial_steps.t: Turn it to the diameter you want to try, measure it and write the diameter down.
trial_steps.why: If you have a calculated blank from one of the other methods, get within 0.001 to 0.002 in (0.03 to 0.05 mm) of it. Hold the blank closely from part to part: 0.0005 in on the blank shows as about 0.001 in on the knurled diameter.

trial_steps.t: Oil the knurls and the work, and set a slow speed.
trial_steps.why: The sources differ on speed. For small manual lathes: about 100 rpm for 1/2 in of soft material (Sherline), 150 to 200 rpm (pjsminilathe). For production knurling GenSwiss gives an upper limit of about 150 sfm (50 m/min), and about 50 sfm (15 m/min) for harder steels and stainless. Start slow.

trial_steps.t: Bring the knurl up until it just touches, add light pressure and turn the spindle by hand about two turns.
trial_steps.why: A light first impression shows whether the knurl tracks before the piece is spoiled.

trial_steps.t: Look at the marks: one clean set of lines, even across the width of the wheel, means it tracks.
trial_steps.why: Tracking is usually settled after one full turn of the part. A second set of lines between the first is double tracking.

trial_steps.t: If it double tracks, first try a firmer first bite. If it still does, change the blank by about 0.005 in (0.13 mm), up or down, and start again at step 2.
trial_steps.why: More infeed usually cures double tracking on bump and cut knurling (GenSwiss). The 0.005 in step is Dorian's for a knurl that double tracks; Sherline gives the same amount, up or down, for a diameter that does not knurl properly.

trial_steps.t: When it tracks, start the spindle and go to full depth in as few turns as you can, with plenty of oil.
trial_steps.why: Bump knurling: 0.001 to 0.004 in per revolution (0.025 to 0.1 mm), finished in 5 to 20 revolutions (GenSwiss). Oil washes the chips out and keeps the knurls from seizing on their pins (Hoffman).

trial_steps.t: Measure the knurled diameter and enter it below to get the growth.
trial_steps.why: Form knurling raises the diameter by an amount that depends on pitch, material and depth; cut knurling barely changes it. The makers' allowance tables are approximate, so the trial piece is the measure.

trial_steps.t: Write down the blank, speed and growth that worked for this knurl and material.
trial_steps.why: BenchMate's advice: the next job with the same knurl and material then starts from a diameter that is known to track.
